summary: This is the React documentation page "Your First Component" from the Learn React section. It explains that components are reusable UI building blocks and that a React component is a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns JSX markup. It walks through defining a Profile component with export default, a Gallery component that nests several Profile components, and a warning never to define a component inside another component. The page ends with a recap and four challenges.
one_line: React docs page explaining components as reusable JavaScript functions that return JSX, with examples of defining, exporting, and nesting them.
key_facts: Components are one of the core concepts of React and the foundation upon which you build user interfaces (UI).
React lets you combine markup, CSS, and JavaScript into custom "components", reusable UI elements for your app.
A React component is a JavaScript function that you can sprinkle with markup.
The export default prefix is a standard JavaScript syntax (not specific to React) that lets you mark the main function in a file so you can later import it from other files.
React component names must start with a capital letter or they won't work.
The JSX syntax lets you embed markup inside JavaScript; the img tag in the example is written like HTML but is actually JavaScript under the hood.
If markup isn't all on the same line as the return keyword, you must wrap it in a pair of parentheses; without them, code on the lines after return will be ignored.
In the Gallery example, the Gallery component renders three Profile components inside a section element with the heading "Amazing scientists".
Lowercase tags like <section> refer to HTML tags, while capitalized tags like <Profile /> refer to components.
Components must never be defined inside another component; the page says doing so is very slow and causes bugs.
When a child component needs data from a parent, it should be passed by props instead of nesting definitions.
Most React apps use components all the way down, including larger pieces like sidebars, lists, and complete pages.
The page cites Chakra UI and Material UI as examples of community component libraries that can jumpstart a project.
The Recap states that in a React app every piece of UI is a component, and components are regular JavaScript functions whose names begin with a capital letter and which return JSX markup.
The page includes four challenges: Export the component, Fix the return statement, Spot the mistake, and Your own component.
